Africa’s water crisis is constraining growth through floods, droughts, and pollution, according to BCG’s assessment. The central challenge is not a lack of potential solutions, but turning localized risks into investable, coordinated infrastructure programs that deliver resilience and economic returns.

Water risks are severe but concentrated in identifiable hotspotsHeavy rainfall affected 11 million people across 27 African countries in 2024, while drought and poor sanitation compound losses in distinct basins, cities, and economic corridors.

Water infrastructure can address all three risks at onceDrainage, storage, treatment, and sanitation systems simultaneously reduce flood damage, improve supply reliability, and protect water quality. Yet climate-resilient water and sanitation investment faces a $30 billion annual funding gap.

Closing the investment gap could generate an outsized economic dividendClosing the gap could unlock $200 billion in annual economic gains by reducing losses and raising productivity; each dollar invested in water and sanitation can return about $4.30.

The binding constraint is delivery, not the availability of solutionsSouth Africa illustrates the problem: weak maintenance, fragmented mandates, distorted pricing, and limited private capital prevent viable interventions from becoming scalable programs. Governments and businesses must build bankable pipelines, blend finance, and coordinate stakeholders.

Executive Summary
Water Risk Is Already Holding Back Growth
Africa’s water challenge is best understood through three connected lenses: too much water (flood risk), too little water (scarcity and reliability), and water that is too dirty (degrading quality and polluted water resources). These risks reinforce each other. Together they are damaging infrastructure, disrupting supply chains, weakening public services, displacing communities and constraining growth.The costs are already visible. Africa spends ~2–5% of GDP a year responding to climate extremes. More than 400 million people lack access to safe water and ~800 million lack basic hygiene. Inadequate sanitation costs ~$200 billion in lost economic value every year, and ~115 deaths an hour are linked to unsafe water and sanitation.Risk Concentrates in a Limited Set of Hotspots
The most important insight is that water risks are not evenly distributed. They are concentrated in a limited set of basins, cities and economic corridors, and flood, drought and water quality risks each follow a different geography (see Exhibit 1).

Flooding remains one of the most visible risks. In 2024, heavy rainfall affected ~11 million people across 27 African countries, causing ~4 million displacements and around 2,500 fatalities. Flood risk is particularly concentrated along coastal and riverine systems in West, North and parts of Central Africa, where high population density and economic activity amplify the impact. Egypt ranks first in the world for riverine flood risk, and Egypt, Nigeria and Sudan are among the world’s most-exposed countries to riverine and coastal flooding.Drought is slower-moving but equally severe. It has caused more than $70 billion in losses in Africa over the past 50 years and accounts for up to 88% of disaster-related impacts in some regions. Arid and semi-arid regions in North, East and Southern Africa are most affected. Somalia ranks first globally for drought risk, and Zimbabwe, Namibia, Mauritania and South Africa also sit in the global top five.Water quality and sanitation challenges impose persistent costs. Around 70% of Africa’s population lacks access to safely managed sanitation. Water quality risks are concentrated in regions with limited sanitation infrastructure and rapid urbanization, particularly parts of West and Central Africa.Because water risks are localized, investment should follow a strategic approach that focuses on the high-risk hotspots where interventions can deliver the greatest impact.

A Significant, Addressable Investment Opportunity
Across all three lenses, water infrastructure is the common enabling layer. Flood resilience depends on drainage systems, flood defenses and early warning infrastructure. Drought resilience relies on storage, diversification and efficient distribution systems. Water quality improvements require treatment plants, sanitation systems and circular water infrastructure. Investing in resilient water infrastructure therefore reduces risk across all three lenses at once.Flood resilience in Africa’s ten highest flood-risk countries requires ~$31 billion by 2030 (see Exhibit 2). Egypt tops the list at $17.86 billion, or 58% of the total, driven by high exposure to both riverine flooding along the Nile and coastal risk. Nigeria and Sudan follow. Both face recurrent large-scale riverine flooding, which calls for river-basin flood management, early warning systems and resilient urban drainage.

Drought resilience requires ~$1.2 billion to 2030 across Africa’s ten highest drought-risk countries (see Exhibit 3). South Africa and Kenya make up 70% of this, as that is where exposure and drought probability overlap most. The biggest needs are in measures that stabilize supply and demand, such as efficiency, diversified supply (including reuse where relevant), groundwater management, and early warning and early action.

The largest requirement is in WASH. Building climate-resilient water and sanitation infrastructure requires ~$50 billion a year. Current investment flows are ~$20 billion a year, leaving an annual gap of ~$30 billion. Closing this gap could unlock ~$200 billion in annual economic gains, equivalent to a ~5% GDP uplift for Africa. UNICEF cites a return of ~$4.30 for every $1 invested in WASH. These investments reduce losses, improve productivity and unlock economic value across sectors.Lessons From South Africa: The Constraint Is Delivery
South Africa provides a useful example of how Africa’s water resilience challenge can be translated into a delivery problem. The country faces a multidimensional water challenge that spans scarcity, infrastructure deterioration, flood risk and water quality degradation. In practice, the core problem is an inability to consistently convert water risk into investable, executable programs, rather than an absence of interventions.Nine systemic challenges act together as binding constraints on delivery: lack of private investment into water infrastructure; limited integration of existing tools and models; political interference in water management; inaccurate water pricing; limited preparedness for future climate impacts; complex governance with overlapping mandates; weak strategic planning and water allocation; limited maintenance budgets for ageing infrastructure; and slow implementation of water infrastructure.Three lessons stand out. Solutions must be translated into prioritized and investable pipelines, rather than left as disconnected projects. Delivery requires both capital mobilization and institutional strengthening, not one without the other. And stakeholder coordination is a core condition for scale. While the risk profile and institutional context will differ by country, Africa needs a repeatable model for turning water risk into bankable, scalable resilience programs.Making the Opportunity Bankable
The next frontier for Africa is scalable, multifunctional solutions: interventions that address water resilience, adaptation and mitigation at the same time. Examples include sponge cities, which reduce flood risk and water scarcity; living breakwaters, which reduce coastal flood and erosion risk; solar-covered canals, which reduce evaporation while generating renewable energy; and wastewater plants that capture methane for energy and recover nutrients. These solutions can also access dual-benefit finance, which grew from $18 billion in 2018 to $58 billion in 2023, nearly matching adaptation flows of $65 billion.Public and private actors can capture value from these solutions through three pathways (see Exhibit 4). The first is direct resilience: investment that protects operations, public services and supply chains from water-related risks while reducing sectoral emissions. The second is revenue, where adaptation and mitigation benefits have paying customers, through user fees, payments for ecosystem services, insurance premiums or carbon credits. The third is asset-value uplift, where restoring ecosystems or improving community environments increases the value of surrounding land and property.

Scaling these solutions requires co-benefits designed in from the outset, cross-sector collaboration, financial innovation such as blended finance and guarantees to reduce risk, and inclusive governance that meaningfully involves affected communities. Governments can align climate and water planning, direct public finance towards integrated outcomes, develop regulatory and taxonomy frameworks that recognize multifunctional outcomes, and strengthen institutional capacity. Businesses can redesign core operations, integrate climate and water objectives into business planning, prioritize investments with measurable outcomes, and collaborate with governments, other businesses, communities and civil society.

Turning Water Risk into a Resilience Dividend
Africa’s water challenge is no longer primarily a question of what to build, but of how to organize for delivery. Capital will flow where risks are understood, responsibilities are clear, projects are well prepared and benefits can be measured. By creating bankable pipelines and coordinated delivery platforms, African countries can convert water risk from a growing liability into an engine of resilience, investment and inclusive growth.
